title: Business Valuation
outcomes: Apply asset, income and cash-flow valuation approaches.
Estimate cost of equity and beta for unlisted firms.
Use relative valuation and the chop-shop method.
Value distressed firms, start-ups and digital platforms and consider ESG.

meta.exam_tip: State the approach, justify it for the business, and show unlever-relever steps clearly.

concepts.title: Valuation approaches: asset, income and cash flow
body: Business valuation estimates the economic worth of a business for transactions, fund-raising, regulation, litigation or reporting. Key tools: present value, IRR, return on investment, and terminal value (often via the Gordon growth formula TV = CF × (1 + g) ÷ (k − g), or an exit multiple).
Asset-based approach: net asset value (book or adjusted), net realisable value (liquidation) and replacement value — suits holding companies, asset-heavy or loss-making firms.

Income approach: P/E or earnings yield multipliers and capitalisation of maintainable earnings. Cash-flow approach: discount FCFF at WACC (deduct debt for equity value) or FCFE at Ke, with explicit forecasts and a terminal value.
concepts.analogy: Assets show what it owns, earnings what it makes, cash flows what it is worth.
concepts.work: A property-holding company is often valued on adjusted net assets.

concepts.title: Cost of equity and beta for unlisted companies
body: Cost of equity: CAPM (Rf + β × MRP), or arbitrage pricing with several factors.

Unlisted companies lack market betas: take comparables' equity betas, unlever them to asset beta βa = βe ÷ [1 + (1 − t)D/E] (debt beta zero), average, and relever at the target's capital structure βe = βa × [1 + (1 − t)D/E]. Adjust for size, liquidity and company-specific risk premiums.
Discount rates must match cash flows and currency.
concepts.analogy: Borrow the risk from listed peers, then adjust for your own debt.
concepts.work: Lower target leverage gives a lower relevered beta.

concepts.title: Relative valuation and chop-shop
body: Relative valuation values a business by comparison: P/E, price-to-book, EV/EBITDA, EV/sales, and sector-specific multiples (per subscriber, per tonne). Steps: choose comparables, compute multiples, adjust for differences in growth, risk and size, and apply to the target.

The chop-shop method values a diversified company as if broken up: value each segment using industry multiples of pure-play firms, sum them, and compare with market value to detect a conglomerate discount.
concepts.analogy: Value it like its peers — piece by piece if necessary.
concepts.work: A conglomerate trading below the sum of its parts may be a break-up target.

concepts.title: Value-based measures: EVA, MVA and SVA
body: Economic value added (EVA) = NOPAT − (capital employed × WACC): profit after charging for all capital. Positive EVA means value creation; it can drive incentives.
Market value added (MVA) = market value of the firm (or equity) − capital invested by providers; it reflects the market's view of present value of future EVAs.

Shareholder value analysis (SVA) uses value drivers — sales growth, operating margin, tax rate, investment in fixed and working capital, planning period and cost of capital — to compute shareholder value from free cash flows.
concepts.analogy: Profit is not value until it beats the cost of capital.
concepts.work: NOPAT of 150 on capital of 1,000 at 12% WACC gives EVA of 30.

concepts.title: Special situations: distress, start-ups, digital platforms and ESG
body: Fair value is a market-participant, arm's-length price; going-concern value assumes continued operations, while non-going concern (liquidation) value assumes break-up. Distressed companies may be valued with modified DCF (probability-weighted scenarios), DCF plus distress value, APV, or relative valuation with distress-adjusted multiples.

Start-ups lack history and profits; value drivers include team, market size, traction and IP. Methods: Berkus, cost-to-duplicate, comparable transactions, scorecard, First Chicago (weighted scenarios) and venture capital method (post-money value = exit value ÷ (1 + target return)^n; pre-money = post-money − investment).

Digital platforms are valued on users, engagement, network effects and unit economics using income, market and cost approaches. ESG factors affect valuation through cash flows (costs, revenues, regulation) and discount rates (risk perception).
concepts.analogy: Unusual businesses need adapted methods and judgement.
concepts.work: A VC targeting 40% return values a start-up by discounting its expected exit value.

illustrations.title: Beta for an unlisted firm
illustrations.q: A listed comparable has equity beta 1.5 and debt-to-equity 0.5. The unlisted target will have debt-to-equity 0.3. Tax rate 25%; risk-free rate 7%; market risk premium 6%. Assuming debt beta is zero, compute the target's cost of equity.

illustrations.title: EVA and terminal value
illustrations.q: (a) Jade Ltd. has EBIT of ₹200 crore, tax rate 25%, capital employed ₹1,000 crore and WACC 12%. Compute EVA. (b) Its free cash flow to firm in year 5 is ₹80 crore, growing at 5% thereafter. Compute the terminal value at the end of year 5.

viva.q: Name the three broad valuation approaches.
viva.model: Asset-based, income-based (earnings) and cash-flow based (DCF) approaches.

viva.q: How do you estimate beta for an unlisted company?
viva.model: Unlever comparable listed companies' betas to asset betas, average them and relever at the target's debt-equity ratio.
Valuing a business by applying multiples such as P/E or EV/EBITDA from comparable companies or transactions.

viva.q: What does a positive EVA indicate?
viva.model: The business earns more than the cost of all the capital employed, so it creates value.

viva.q: Why are traditional methods hard to apply to start-ups?
viva.model: They have little history, negative profits and uncertain cash flows, so value depends on qualitative drivers and scenarios.

cases.title: BrightPath EdTech
cases.case: A VC plans to invest ₹20 crore in BrightPath EdTech, expecting an exit value of ₹300 crore in 5 years and a target return of 50% a year. A diversified parent of BrightPath has two divisions: education (EBITDA ₹40 crore; peer EV/EBITDA 12) and printing (EBITDA ₹30 crore; peer 6). The parent's EV is ₹580 crore.

mcqs.q: Post-money value of BrightPath (₹ crore, nearest whole):
mcqs.explain: 300 ÷ 1.5^5 = 300 ÷ 7.59 = 39.5. In practice: target return is high.
